item.title: Rate-Optimal Quantum Discrete Simulation Optimization
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Quantum discrete simulation optimization has minimax expected optimality gap Ω(|𝒳|/T), achieved up to logarithmic factors by the textscQUEST algorithm (O(|𝒳|log⁡T/T)). Convergence rate improves quadratically over budget T compared to classical bound Ω(|𝒳|/T), with worse scaling in decision count |𝒳|.

Grade 0.462 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Mingjie Hu, Jian-Qiang Hu

Figure

Expected optimality gap as a function of simulation budget T under Bernoulli outcomes with |𝒳|=20. Compares the faster decay of the quantum textscQUEST algorithm against the classical textscMC-EST baseline.

Asks

How does quantum computing affect the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization in the fixed-budget setting, and can a provably rate-optimal algorithm be designed?

Before

Classical discrete simulation optimization has minimax expected optimality gap lower bound Ω(|𝒳|/T).

But

Fixed-budget setting with discrete candidate decisions |𝒳|. Continuous observation outputs require finite support discretization onto grid qubits.

Tools

sequential quantum phase-testing lower bound reduction · quantum Monte Carlo estimation · sequential elimination framework · slow-measurement mechanism · Qiskit numerical simulation

Abstract

Quantum computing has developed rapidly in recent years and has shown potential advantages over classical computing in various domains. In this paper, we study whether quantum computing can accelerate the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization in the fixed-budget setting. We first formulate the quantum discrete simulation optimization problem by defining the quantum simulation oracle, the algorithmic performance measure, and the corresponding optimality guarantee. Based on this formulation, we establish a minimax lower bound on the expected optimality gap for any quantum algorithm. The lower bound analysis reduces the discrete simulation optimization problem to a sequential quantum phase-testing problem, and the resulting lower-bound argument may be of independent interest. By comparing the quantum lower bound with its classical counterpart, we show that the optimal convergence rate in the quantum setting exhibits a quadratic improvement in its dependence on the simulation budget, at the cost of a worse dependence on the number of decisions. We then propose the first fixed-budget quantum algorithm, called textscQUEST, for discrete simulation optimization. The algorithm combines a quantum Monte Carlo subroutine with a sequential elimination framework and uses a slow-measurement mechanism to help preserve quantum superposition during the optimization process. We prove that textscQUEST achieves the optimal convergence rate up to logarithmic factors. Numerical experiments further show that textscQUEST outperforms its classical counterpart, which provides empirical evidence for the quantum advantage in improving the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization algorithms.

item.title: Breaking the chain: geometry-native state preparation with ASPIRE
item.description:
Worth a look new method — ASPIRE generates state-preparation circuits by greedily disentangling qubit pairs based on entanglement geometry and hardware connectivity, achieving shallower circuit depths and higher fidelities than standard nearest-neighbour sequential staircase compilation.

Grade 0.440 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Fredrik Hasselgren, Matthew L. Sims-Goh

Asks

How to compile shallow, high-fidelity state-preparation circuits for structured quantum states by exploiting native hardware connectivity and non-local entanglement geometry?

Before

Approximate MPS compilation relied on layered sequential staircases of nearest-neighbour gates.

But

Heuristic greedy gate selection; demonstrated on numerical simulations of Hamiltonian ground states and amplitude-encoded functions under NISQ and early fault-tolerant settings.

Tools

Adaptive State Preparation by Iterative Removal of Entanglement (ASPIRE) · Matrix product states (MPS) · Entanglement removability scoring · Circuit synthesis under hardware connectivity constraints

Abstract

Loading data into quantum computers is a key bottleneck that threatens end-to-end quantum advantage. Quantum-circuit compilers for structured states like matrix product states (MPS) are a critical enabler to manage this in quantum chemistry, finance, and many-body quantum simulation. Approximate preparation of MPS typically relies on layered sequential staircases of nearest-neighbour gates. We present Adaptive State Preparation by Iterative Removal of Entanglement (ASPIRE), an algorithm that approximately compiles state-preparation circuits by selecting gates based on the state's underlying entanglement geometry and the available connectivity of the target quantum processor. Our protocol scores candidate qubit pairs on the removability of their entanglement and identifies layers of parallelised long-ranged gates that remove the most entanglement. We demonstrate our protocol empirically across a range of settings, illustrating its success for preparing Hamiltonian ground states and multivariate amplitude-encoded functions, and accounting for qubit connectivity, hardware noise, and both NISQ and early fault-tolerant settings. Throughout, ASPIRE typically achieves higher fidelities and shallower circuits than existing methods for states with long-ranged entanglement, even when classical optimisation is accounted for. Our investigation positions ASPIRE as a competitive, resource-frugal state-preparation protocol, with particular promise for applications tolerant to imperfect fidelity such as preparation of guide states for quantum phase estimation.

item.title: Quantum algorithms for orthogonal polynomial transforms
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Constructs quantum orthogonal polynomial transforms (QOPT) running in O(polylog(N,1/ϵ)) time for discrete Charlier, Meixner, and Krawtchouk transforms, and for continuous Laguerre transforms. Achieves an O(Npolylog⁡((N+α+β+1)/ϵ)) runtime for the discrete Hahn transform.

Grade 0.429 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Anupam Prakash, Shree Hari Sureshbabu, Dylan Herman, Shouvanik Chakrabarti

Figure

Hierarchical chart of the Askey scheme of hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials showing the limit transitions between polynomial families and their achieved quantum transform complexities.

Asks

Which orthogonal polynomial transforms admit efficient quantum circuit implementations with exponential speedups over classical transforms?

Before

Hermite transform runs in poly-logarithmic time (Jain et al. STOC'26); naive Hahn transform is O(N2).

But

Preserves orthogonality approximately up to an energy cutoff; assumes integer parameters for Jacobi-to-Hahn reduction; Wilson, Racah, continuous Hahn, and continuous dual Hahn families not solved.

Tools

Wei–Norman factorization / Fast-forwarding · Gaussian optical gates on Cartesian grids · SU(2) and SU(1,1) Schwinger representations · 3-term chirp decomposition · Quantum Hankel Transform / FFTLog

Abstract

A quantum orthogonal polynomial transform (QOPT) is an algorithmic primitive that maps a superposition of standard basis states ∑_k α_k |k⟩ coherently to a basis of normalized univariate polynomials orthogonal with respect to a probability measure μ(x). We provide new discrete and continuous QOPTs for polynomial families in the Askey scheme extending the results for the quantum Hermite transform (Jain et al., STOC'26). Our efficient QOPT algorithms require time O(polylog(N, 1/ε)), where N is the grid size and ε is the error, for the discrete Charlier, Meixner and Krawtchouk transforms and for the integer-order Laguerre transform in the continuous setting. The efficient QOPTs are obtained by uncovering the links between Askey scheme polynomials and Gaussian quantum optical gates and developing a compilation framework for SU(2) and SU(1,1) optical gates on Cartesian grids extending the framework developed by Iyer et al. (arXiv:2602.15180). Further, we reduce the continuous Jacobi transform to the discrete Hahn transform and provide an O (Npolylog((N+α+β+1)/ε))-time Hahn transform, a quadratic speedup over the naive implementation. This is based on a more efficient compilation of the Clebsch--Gordan transform for coupling SU(2) representations with spins (j₁, j₂). Finally, we develop a new framework for Laguerre transforms for all orders ν>0 by fast-forwarding the corresponding radial oscillator using a 3-term chirp decomposition and an efficient algorithm for the Quantum Hankel Transform on a logarithmic grid.

item.title: Unitary complexity in polynomial space
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Every unitary 𝒰∈𝗎𝗇𝗂𝗍𝖺𝗋𝗒𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤 satisfies either 𝒰∉𝗎𝗇𝗂𝗍𝖺𝗋𝗒𝖯𝖠𝖫𝖫 or 𝒰∈𝗎𝗇𝗂𝗍𝖺𝗋𝗒𝖯𝖥𝖭𝖤𝖷𝖯. Consequently, existence of quantum commitments implies either no polynomial-time unitary synthesis or 𝖡𝖯𝖯≠𝖭𝖤𝖷𝖯.

Grade 0.419 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · William Kretschmer, Ewin Tang

Asks

Does the hardness underlying quantum cryptography imply breakthrough classical complexity lower bounds?

But

Garbage-allowed implementations vs. garbage-free implementations coincide up to tensoring with the adjoint.

Tools

unitary complexity classes (unitaryP, unitaryPSPACE) · unitary synthesis reductions · projective unitary dilations and garbage-state tracking

Abstract

We show that if quantum commitments exist, then either there is no polynomial-time solution to the unitary synthesis problem, or BPP ≠NEXP. Thus, showing unconditionally that quantum commitments exist would require answering at least one of two longstanding open questions in complexity theory. We prove our main result as a consequence of a more general lemma, which shows that every unitary in unitaryPSPACE either cannot be synthesized efficiently relative to any classical oracle, or can be synthesized efficiently with an oracle for NEXP search problems. Our lemma has other noteworthy consequences, including that certain oracle separations involving unitaryPSPACE would imply breakthrough classical lower bounds such as NC ≠NP. Along the way, we propose new definitions for the unitary complexity classes unitaryP and unitaryPSPACE. Our changes address the biggest conceptual issues with definitions suggested in prior work, and lead to elegant proofs. We study both implementations that erase garbage and implementations that allow it, because we cannot rule out the possibility that the two definitions differ. Nevertheless, we show that both definitions can be viewed as special cases of each other. We also showcase many other ways in which our definitions are robust. For example, we show that unitaryPSPACE has an equivalent characterization as the set of unitary transformations whose entries can be computed to arbitrary precision in polynomial space. Consequently, we deduce that unitaryPSPACE can generically erase garbage, a result that provably fails relative to unitary oracles.

item.title: Exponential lower bounds on the fermionic Gaussian rank of magic states and the bosonic coherent state rank of Fock states
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Fermionic Gaussian rank of |M⟩⊗k is lower bounded by 89(k+1)(27(8+27)256)k>89(k+1)1.4018k, with δ-approximate rank bounded by (1−δ2) times this value. Coherent state border rank of n-mode bosonic Fock state |m⟩ is exactly ∏j=1n(1+mj).

Grade 0.411 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations” · Oliver Reardon-Smith

Figure

Exact fermionic Gaussian rank of |M⟩⊗k plotted against number of copies k, comparing the asymptotic analytical lower bound, the small-k optimized lower bound, the k=2 bound, and the 2k upper bound.

Asks

What are the exact and approximate rank lower bounds for decomposing magic states into fermionic Gaussian states and Fock states into bosonic coherent states?

Before

For fermionic Gaussian rank of |M⟩⊗k, only trivial lower bound of 2 was known for k≥2. For coherent-state border rank of |1⟩⊗n, superpolynomial but sub-exponential lower bounds were proved by prior work.

But

Pure states of fixed parity. Fermionic rank bound established for the four-qubit magic state |M⟩=12(|0000⟩+|1111⟩) and products thereof. Bosonic lower bound applies to coherent states, not the full set of bosonic Gaussian states.

Tools

matrix rank method · Majorana operator polynomial evaluations · Hankel-type matrix representations · Frobenius and Schatten norms

Abstract

Recent algorithms for classical simulation of quantum mechanics have runtime whose superpolynomial component is given by a linear dependence on the number of terms required to write large tensor products of certain "magic" states as superpositions of "free" states (which may be stabilizer states, fermionic Gaussian states or others). Surprisingly little is known about the number of terms in such decompositions, called ranks (e.g. the stabilizer rank, fermionic-Gaussian rank etc.). For complexity theoretic reasons they are expected to grow exponentially in the number of tensor factors but, while exponential upper bounds are known for both the stabilizer and fermionic-Gaussian rank of magic states; the best known lower bounds on the stabiliser rank are quadratic, and no bounds on the fermionic-Gaussian rank are known beyond fixed constants. In this work we prove that any fermionic Gaussian decomposition of |M⟩^(⊗k) consists of Ω(1.4^k) terms. Here |M⟩ is the most standard magic state for fermionic linear optics: the 4 qubit state that may be consumed to implement a swap gate. We also prove essentially matching bounds on the δ-approximate rank of the same state, lower bounding it by the same quantity that bounds the exact rank, multiplied by a factor of 1-δ². Our results on exact fermionic Gaussian rank apply directly to any product of k fixed parity non-Gaussian states, although the same is not true of the approximate rank. Finally, we prove that the coherent state border rank of an n-mode bosonic Fock state with m_j bosons in mode j is exactly ∏_j(1+m_j), answering a conjecture of Ref. [1] and obtain lower bounds on the approximate coherent state rank given by the same quantity multiplied by a function of the fidelity of the approximation, emphasizing the broad applicability of the method we employ.

item.title: Exponential quantum space advantage in random data streams
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Streaming Yamakawa–Zhandry Code Intersection in random order takes poly(n) qubits versus exp⁡(nΩ(1)) classical bits. Streaming Optimal Polynomial Intersection to target value ⌈n/2+dn/8⌉ takes O(dlog⁡n) qubits versus Ω(n) classical bits.

Grade 0.411 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Adam Bouland, Matthew Ding, Siddhartha Jain

Asks

Can quantum algorithms achieve exponential advantage for space complexity in the streaming model when inputs are presented in a uniformly random order?

But

Asymptotic regime with d=ω(log⁡n) and d=o(n/log⁡n) for Optimal Polynomial Intersection; random oracle setting; applies to streaming memory constraints, not general query complexity.

Tools

density-restoring partitions · convex potential functions on read-once branching programs · decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) · folded Reed–Solomon list-recoverability

Abstract

We show two unconditional quantum space advantages in the random-order streaming model. First, we show the Yamakawa--Zhandry Code Intersection problem admits exponential quantum advantage in the streaming model when its inputs are streamed in random order. This means quantum computers exhibit exponential space advantage even when simply receiving (x,f(x)) pairs for a uniformly random function f in a uniformly random order. item.title: Root-sparsity scaling for Hamiltonian simulation, differential equations and linear-system solvers
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Simulates s-sparse Hamiltonians in 𝒪(sτ+sτlog⁡(1/ε)+log⁡(1/ε)) queries for τ=η|t|, dissipative linear ODEs in 𝒪(g‾sτlog⁡(Cg‾/ε)), and linear systems in 𝒪(sκlog⁡(1/ε)).

Grade 0.405 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations” · Dominic W. Berry, Abhishek Rawat, Sophia Simon, Guang Hao Low

Asks

Can quantum algorithms achieve exact square-root sparsity scaling for general sparse Hamiltonian simulation, linear ODEs, and linear system solvers without subpolynomial overheads?

Before

Linear-in-s scaling for standard block encodings; previous general s Hamiltonian simulation required subpolynomial factors from an iterated interaction picture (Low 2019) or conditional norm assumptions (Berry and Childs 2012).

But

Requires sparse oracle access with row/column Euclidean norm bounds η, certified time discretisation for time-dependent cases, and efficient entry decoding circuits for gate implementations.

Tools

exact entrywise Cayley representation · Cayley transducers · Chebyshev filter · linear combination of Hamiltonian simulations (LCHS) · ordered-rotation factorisation

Abstract

We give quantum algorithms for Hamiltonian simulation, linear differential equations, and linear systems with square-root dependence on sparsity. For an s-sparse Hermitian matrix with row and column Euclidean norms bounded by η, evolution for time t to error ε uses O(√sτ+√sτlog(1/ε)+log(1/ε)) queries, where τ=η|t|. The same bound holds for time-dependent Hamiltonians with coherent time-indexed sparse access and certified time discretisation. Our construction combines an exact entrywise representation with Cayley transducers. A joint lower bound nearly matches the time, sparsity, and precision dependence, ruling out a uniformly additive bound in √sτ and log(1/ε). For dissipative linear differential equations we obtain O(barg[√s(τ+√τ)+1]log(Cbarg/ε)) queries, where τ is the evolution time multiplied by a norm bound, barg bounds the ratio of combined input and source norms to the final-solution norm, and C is an absolute constant. We sharpen this bound by separating Hamiltonian and dissipative components, and treat general constant generators. Lower bounds capture joint parameter dependence for time-dependent equations and precision hardness for constant positive semidefinite dissipation. For linear systems, a Cayley walk and Chebyshev filter give O(κ√slog(1/ε)) queries when |A|≤1 and |A⁻¹|≤κ, and we give an alternative proof of a matching joint lower bound. We also give gate-efficient implementations of time-independent Hamiltonian simulation and the dissipative ODE solver, including Lipschitz time dependence, retaining the query bounds with polylogarithmic overhead in inverse precision given efficient entry decoding, arithmetic, and required source preparations.
